extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, policymakers and communicators interested in COVID-19 misinformation and responses
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of COVID-19 misinformation ('infodemic'): types of false claims, examples (fake cures, conspiracies), actors (public figures, platforms, governments), and institutional responses (WHO, regulators, publishers, fact-checkers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public statements must be based on scientific evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Public figures, including politicians, should be 'extra careful' when making statements about cures or treatments and must say things that are 'based on some scientific evidence'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements about cures or treatment claims 'have such a huge following' and 'has to be backed by evidence.' Avoid making or amplifying unverified medical claims; leave such claims to qualified experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow authoritative clinical guidance for treatments (ivermectin example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Major health authorities advise limits on use of specific treatments: 'WHO advises that ivermectin only be used to treat COVID-19 within clinical trials'; 'EMA advises against use of ivermectin for the prevention or treatment of COVID-19 outside randomised clinical trials'; FDA warns 'Why You Should Not Use Ivermectin to Treat or Prevent COVID-19.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications and claims about therapeutics should align with WHO/EMA/FDA/NIH/IDSA guidance and note when evidence is insufficient or limited to clinical-trial contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not market or promote unapproved 'miracle' cures; regulators will act
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators (FDA, state attorneys general) issue warnings and take enforcement action against entities and individuals selling toxic or unapproved products marketed as COVID-19 cures (e.g., warning letters, lawsuits, prison sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases or promotional materials must not claim cures without evidence and appropriate approvals; sellers of unapproved products risk legal action and public-health harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platforms and publishers should remove or limit misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media companies and publishers took actions such as removing posts, taking down content, and dropping paywalls for COVID-19 coverage to limit the spread of misinformation and increase access to authoritative information ('Facebook says it has taken down 7 million posts'; 'Major Publishers Take Down Paywalls').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform policies and editorial decisions should prioritize evidence-based content, fact-checking, and demotion/removal of demonstrably false health claims during an infodemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and cite fact-checking and authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple fact-checking organizations and news agencies (AFP Fact Check, Snopes, Reuters Fact Check, PolitiFact, WHO Mythbusters) are cited as counters to false claims and viral myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rebutting or describing claims, cite reputable fact-checks and primary authoritative sources (WHO, peer-reviewed studies, official regulator statements) rather than repeating unverified assertions without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share research data and findings relevant to outbreak response
rubrics_metrics.description: Initiatives encouraged rapid sharing of research data and findings relevant to COVID-19 (e.g., Wellcome’s 'Sharing research data and findings relevant to the novel coronavirus' press release).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers, institutions, and journals should facilitate rapid, open sharing of data and results during outbreaks to inform evidence-based responses; press communications should reference shared data and link to sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists and media should avoid amplifying conspiracy theories and unverified remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage that amplifies conspiracy theories, pseudoscience (e.g., fake remedies, miracle cures), or false predictions can mainstream harmful beliefs and lead to real-world harms (examples: runs on animal medicine, hospitalization from TikTok 'remedies', promotion by public figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should contextualize claims, seek expert perspectives, avoid sensationalizing unverified treatments, and link to authoritative guidance rather than merely repeating viral content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer protection and public warnings about scams
rubrics_metrics.description: International and national bodies (UN, FTC, FCC, national health agencies) issued consumer warnings and safety tips against COVID-19 scams and fraudulent products ('COVID-19 Consumer Warnings and Safety Tips'; 'UN health agency warns against coronavirus COVID-19 criminal scams').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public communications should include consumer-protection guidance, alert people to common scam tactics, and point to where to report fraud and get verified information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance misinformation control with protection of free expression and human rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Government measures to crack down on 'fake news' during the pandemic led to arrests and raised concerns about censorship and restrictions on free expression across multiple countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and communications aimed at combating misinformation should be careful not to unduly infringe civil liberties; transparency, proportionality, and legal safeguards are important when restricting speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective actions and accountability for harmful communicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Media outlets, regulators and legal systems held individuals and platforms accountable for spreading harmful misinformation (examples: takedowns of podcasts/interviews, lawsuits, regulatory warnings, removal of sellers of fake cures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisations issuing communications should name reliable sources for corrections, document corrective steps taken, and cooperate with regulatory/consumer-protection processes where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on high-quality evidence and be wary of low-quality meta-analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly discussion highlighted that 'meta-analyses based on summary data alone are inherently unreliable' (in the context of ivermectin), and large RCTs and Cochrane reviews provide more reliable evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When summarizing scientific evidence in press or guidance, prefer high-quality systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, and transparent data reporting; flag limitations and retractions where relevant.
